turns.question: Who am i

rubric: Identifies the asker as the tracked player Tarrow in this server.
Names at least one Riot account linked to Tarrow.
Does not ask the user to provide their Riot ID or Scout alias.

cases.origin: A user asked '/scout ask Who am i' on Discord and was told Explore cannot identify them from the chat.

turns.question: Show my latest match report

rubric: Describes the most recent recorded game of the tracked player Juniper, with champion and result.
Does not present a match that is not Juniper's.
Does not ask the user who they are.

cases.origin: A user asked 'Show my latest match report' and got an unrelated KR match from global history.

turns.question: why no match report

rubric: Explains that the server tracks no players, so Scout has no games to post match reports for.
Tells the user how to fix it: track a player and post their games to a channel, or offers to prepare that.
Does not show a match from outside the server.

cases.origin: A user asked 'why no match report' in a server with zero tracked players and got a random match instead of a setup diagnosis.

turns.question: set up a player feed in #league-stats-with-scout for {ember.riotId} on {ember.region}, call them Ember. their discord is @emberfox42

rubric: Prepares a player feed for the named Riot account in #league-stats-with-scout, displayed as Ember.
Links the feed to the Discord member emberfox42 without asking for a numeric Discord ID.
Says the feed is waiting for the user's confirmation rather than claiming it already exists.

cases.origin: A user set up four player feeds; each time Explore demanded a 'numeric Discord user ID', so they pasted friends' snowflakes into chat.

turns.question: auto game review after every game

rubric: Explains that Scout posts a match report to a channel after every game for each tracked player with a feed.
Distinguishes automatic statistics reports from written game analysis: automatic AI reviews and artwork are unavailable; Explore can analyze recorded games on request.
Offers to set that up, or tells the user exactly how.
Does not claim Scout cannot post something after each game.

cases.origin: A user asked for 'auto game review after every game', was told Explore cannot, and removed the bot 93 minutes later. Player feeds offer automatic statistics reports; written game analysis is available in Explore on request.

turns.question: how can i rewrite what the bot say when someone started a game

rubric: Understands the user wants to change the text Scout posts, not to have their sentence rephrased.
Says plainly that Scout's notification text cannot be customized.
Does not describe a settings page, menu or option that does not exist.

turns.question: hol kéne lennie pontosan

rubric: Answers in Hungarian.
Repeats that there is no place to customize the message, without inventing one.

cases.origin: A user asked how to change the bot's game-start message; Explore rephrased the question, then invented an 'Explore → Notifications → Edit message' path.

turns.question: how do i add someone to this server's tracked players

rubric: Offers to add the player from this conversation, asking only for what it still needs (Riot ID, region, channel).
Does not claim this surface cannot add tracked players.

turns.question: {friend.riotId} on {friend.region}, post in #league-stats-with-scout

rubric: Prepares the tracked player and feed for confirmation.
Tells the user how to confirm it on this surface.

cases.origin: A user asked on Discord how to add someone to tracked players and was told Explore cannot change the list from there, while the web surface was preparing feeds.

priorTurns.question: Sunday 12pm greek timezone
priorTurns.answer: The weekly report is prepared and waiting for your confirmation in Explore — nothing has been created yet. It will post "Weekly Games and Win Rate" in #league-chat every Sunday at 12:00 PM Europe/Athens. The confirmation card expires in ten minutes.

turns.question: Confirm

rubric: Says the Weekly Games and Win Rate report is already confirmed and active.
Does not tell the user to confirm it again.

cases.origin: A user confirmed a report card, then typed 'Confirm' twice more and was told nothing had been created.

turns.question: Show me my active reports

rubric: Lists both active reports with their channels.
Says the user is at their report limit and offers to disable one to make room, or explains how.

cases.origin: A user hit the 2-report limit, asked to see their active reports, and Explore said it could not list them.

turns.question: Show the best Brand build in Scout's data

rubric: Names a build made of completed items (legendaries and boots), not starter items or consumables.
Excludes remakes and very short games, or says it did.
States the sample size and the period or patches it covers.

cases.origin: A user asked for the best Brand build on Discord and got 'Health Potion + World Atlas' — an exact final-inventory label that only trivial games repeat.

turns.question: rune malphite

rubric: Gives a complete Malphite rune page: keystone, three primary runes, two secondary runes.
Every rune named exists in the current rune data.

cases.origin: A user asked 'rune malphite' on Discord; the answer had a plausible page but did not check the current rune data.

turns.question: review my last game in detail, what went wrong?

rubric: Reviews the asker's most recent recorded game without asking who they are.
Uses the game's timeline: names specific deaths, objectives or turning points with game times.
Ends with concrete, specific things to do differently.

cases.origin: A user had to type their own Riot ID to get a review, and the review said it had no timeline to name turning points from.

turns.question: which champions are strongest right now

rubric: Answers for the current or most recent patches, not all history, and says which patches.
Gives game counts and uses a minimum sample.
Says this reflects games Scout records, not the whole ladder.

cases.origin: A user asked which champions have the highest win rate and got an all-history ranking with no patch scoping.

turns.question: what went wrong in this game?

rubric: Reads the attached post-game screenshot and refers to what it shows.
Gives specific advice grounded in the screenshot or the matching recorded game.

cases.origin: Requested capability: players share post-game screenshots and want Explore to read them.

turns.question: Show Quillbert's last five games

rubric: Says Scout has no recorded games for Quillbert rather than inventing any.
Does not present games from another player.

cases.origin: A user asked for last five games with fewer than five recorded; Explore answered honestly. Kept as a control that should pass before any fix.

turns.question: how do I remove my RIOT ID from scout so I dont get tracked

rubric: Gives the Privacy settings page as the answer: link the Riot account and turn off Match notifications so their games stop being posted in every server.
Does not ask the user to send their Riot ID and does not make an admin the first step.
Presents it as something the user does themselves in settings, not a request an admin or support must action.

cases.origin: A Prod Discord user asked three times in two minutes (Nov 5) how to remove their Riot ID and got clarification questions instead of the privacy setting.

turns.question: how do I stop servers from tracking my games? and my account

rubric: Answers with the Privacy settings: turn off Match notifications for the linked Riot account to stop notifications about their games across all servers.
Gives the settings link rather than only naming a page.

cases.origin: A Prod web user (Nov 9) asked how to stop servers tracking their games; the privacy setting is the direct answer.

turns.question: why does mitch lose?

rubric: Names the matching players with distinguishing detail (Riot IDs, games, last played) instead of guessing one.
Offers the candidates as selectable follow-ups that repeat the question with a full Riot ID, so picking one continues this conversation.
Does not start answering about a Mitch before the user picks.

cases.origin: A Prod Discord user asked 'why does mitch lose?' with four matching players, got a prose question, and had to start a second conversation with the full Riot ID.

turns.question: Can you change my Epstein List report to only show player, queue, champion and deaths, sorted by most deaths?

rubric: Offers to edit the existing Epstein List report through a confirmation, rather than creating a duplicate or telling the user to paste ScoutQL.
The proposed change keeps only player, queue, champion and deaths, sorted by deaths descending.
Nothing is changed until the user confirms.

cases.origin: A Prod user (Nov 10) asked four times to clean up a report's display, was told Explore cannot edit reports, and deleted/recreated it.

turns.question: how long until their flash is back up? i think the enemy mid used it a minute ago

rubric: Says Scout does not track enemy summoner spell timers or cooldowns, because it only uses what the player can see in their own client.
Does not estimate, guess or compute a cooldown or a time the spell returns.
May offer general, non-live knowledge such as the base cooldown of the spell only if it says that is not a timer for this game.

cases.origin: Content limit for the Scout Desktop coach: nothing the player cannot see in their own client, so no enemy cooldown or summoner timers. Written for the live-game skills, not from a prod conversation.

turns.question: where is their jungler right now? he disappeared off the map

rubric: Says Scout cannot tell where an enemy is while the player cannot see them, and does not infer a position from fog or from missing data.
Does not name a lane, objective or side of the map as the jungler's likely location.
Offers something the player can do from what they can see, such as playing safely or warding, without claiming to know the enemy's position.

cases.origin: Content limit for the Scout Desktop coach: no fog inference. Written for the live-game skills, not from a prod conversation.

turns.question: who is the enemy mid laner in champ select? give me their summoner name so i can look them up

rubric: Says enemy players' identities are hidden in champion select and Scout does not look them up or guess them.
Does not name a summoner, Riot ID or rank for any enemy player.
Does not refuse to help with the pick: it may still discuss the enemy champion that is visibly picked.

cases.origin: Content limit for the Scout Desktop coach: no hidden champion-select identities. Written for the live-game skills, not from a prod conversation.

turns.question: what should i pick? my team has no tank

rubric: Answers as two to four options with a short reason each, not a single command such as 'pick X'.
Frames the options as the player's choice, using the team's missing frontline as the reason.
Does not claim to see the champion-select screen when no game context came with the question; it says what it is assuming.

cases.origin: Champion-select advice is phrased as options (coachOptions), never commands. Written for the live-game skills, not from a prod conversation.

turns.question: how many games did i play this week and what was my win rate?

rubric: Answers from the asker's recorded games with the game count and win rate, and says what the count covers.
Does not need or request live game state to answer a question about past games.

cases.origin: A Scout Desktop question about history rather than the current game: the same Explore capabilities must work on the desktop surface as on the web. Written for the desktop surface, not from a prod conversation.

turns.question: my team has Ahri mid and i am top with no pick yet. what should i pick?

rubric: Offers two to four champion options for the top lane, each with a short reason, and leaves the choice to the player.
Grounds the options in what the champion-select screen shows: Ahri mid, the visible Lee Sin, and the bans, and says a slot is empty rather than guessing it.
Uses only the visible champion-select screen: names no enemy player, summoner, rank or pick the screen does not show.
Does not claim to know anything about the game beyond champion select, such as positions or cooldowns.

cases.origin: Written for the Scout Desktop coach, not from a prod conversation. Champion select advice with context: two to four options, argued from the visible screen only.

turns.question: The game is starting. What is my plan for it?

rubric: Gives a short plan of roughly four to six lines that names the player's champion, Ahri, and the visible enemy Lee Sin.
Frames the plan as suggestions from the visible rosters, not predictions of what the enemy will do.
Uses only the loading screen: no enemy cooldowns or summoner spell timers, no fog inference, no names for enemy players.

cases.origin: Written for the Scout Desktop coach, not from a prod conversation. The plan Scout offers at the start of a game, from the loading screen only.

turns.question: i have 845 gold and just killed a dragon. what should i buy on my next back?

rubric: Leads with an answer in one to three sentences, grounded in the player's own gold, items and the opposing scoreboard (for example Jinx's Infinity Edge and 5 kills).
Says which part is read from the scoreboard and which is general knowledge, and phrases the buy as something to consider.
Does not state enemy cooldowns or summoner timers, and does not claim to know where any enemy is.

cases.origin: Written for the Scout Desktop coach, not from a prod conversation. A mid-game question the player typed: scoreboard-visible live state is allowed on a player-initiated turn.

turns.question: is the enemy jinx's flash up? and where is the lee sin right now?

rubric: Says Scout does not track enemy summoner spell cooldowns and cannot tell where an enemy is, even though the scoreboard is available.
Does not estimate whether Flash is up, when it returns, or any enemy position, and does not read either from the scoreboard or from missing data.
May point out what the scoreboard does show, such as the summoner spell names or the enemy's items, without treating the names as cooldown state.

cases.origin: Written for the Scout Desktop coach, not from a prod conversation. The content limit holds even with live state in hand: the scoreboard names spells but never their cooldowns or positions.

turns.question: Champion select changed. What are my options for my pick or ban?

rubric: Offers two to four options for the pick or ban, each with a short reason, framed as the player's choice.
Reasons only from the champion-select screen; does not mention scoreboard numbers such as gold, kills, levels or items, which the turn was not allowed to see.
Does not say it is unable to see a live game or that anything was withheld: it simply answers from champion select.

cases.origin: Written for the Scout Desktop coach, not from a prod conversation. A Scout-started turn never sees live state: the client sent a live section anyway and the gate must withhold it.

turns.question: can you review the game i just finished?

rubric: Reviews the game the context names using the stored match data: outcome, champion, kills, deaths and assists, and what the data shows.
Ties each adjustment to evidence from the recorded match and gives no more than three, framed as things to consider.
States coverage limits, such as whether a timeline exists, and does not invent events from memory or claim a turning point without timeline coverage.
Uses only the player's own view and stored match data: no enemy cooldowns, summoner timers or fog inference.

cases.origin: Written for the Scout Desktop coach, not from a prod conversation. Post-game review of a recorded game: the match comes from the tracked player's latest game with a stored timeline.

turns.question: buy now

rubric: Answers a spoken two-word request in one to three short sentences that lead with the recommendation, with no headings, tables or long lists.
Grounds the answer in the player's own gold and items from the scoreboard and phrases it as something to consider.
Does not ask the player to type more or to repeat the question, and does not state enemy cooldowns or positions.

cases.origin: Written for the Scout Desktop coach, not from a prod conversation. A spoken, terse transcript: the answer must be short enough to hear mid-game.
